title: One to the Other
author: Adrian Neibauer
summary: Fifth-grade teacher Adrian Neibauer describes a close-reading unit built on Rod Serling's Twilight Zone teleplay The Monsters Are Due on Maple Street, used to teach suspicion, scapegoating and mob mentality. He gives background on Serling's war experience and his use of science fiction to address social evils, then walks through a three-read structure. The first read is reader's theater with highlighting of whatever stands out, the second pairs the Twilight Zone episode with annotation of those highlights, and the third combines independent and collective reading with planned pauses to teach conformity, groupthink, the origin of scapegoat and prejudice theory. He models his own thinking, including a careful look at the title, and reports that students had mature discussions and wrote reflections showing they recognised the dangers of prejudice. A closing resources list offers videos, articles and companion episodes for teachers.
points: Spreading one text across three reads, with a different job for each, let students notice, annotate and finally analyse without being overwhelmed by the twist ending.
Modelling his own highlighting and annotation, without giving correct answers, shows that the only way to close read incorrectly is not to engage at all.
Planned pauses at the first scapegoating and at the first act of violence turned the story into a lesson on conformity and prejudice.
Pairing the printed teleplay with the filmed episode kept engagement high and gave students a shared reference for discussion.
Student reflections showed the transfer he hoped for, that humanity is vulnerable to panic but can choose differently, since not every street is Maple Street.
quotes: I stole a week in-between basal reading modules to teach my students the destructive capabilities of suspicion, xenophobia, and crowd psychology.
The first read is designed for students to pay attention to what their brains notice. I tell students to highlight anything that stands out.
I tell students that the only way to close read incorrectly is not to highlight, think, or pay attention at all.
I pause here to teach students the psychology of conformity and groupthink. I tell them the origin of the word scapegoat and prejudice theory.
Serling explicitly connects science fiction to the real world. He wants us thinking about human truths and how they impact society.
I realize that how I structured this close reading experience and the following discussions over multiple days, better scaffolded students’ understanding of the major themes of the teleplay.
Humanity may be vulnerable to panic and prejudice, but we can make better choices. We are not destined to tear each other apart.
